scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: PANIC from the night shift -- an alert popped up and
now everyone is convinced one of the big routers in the middle of the network
(R6? maybe R7?) CRASHED overnight and is just eating all the traffic going to
the far side. It has obviously gone down and everything crossing the middle
is dying inside it!! Please go and reboot the crashed one (whichever it is)
and tell us it's fixed!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The night-shift alarm claiming that r6 or r7 crashed and is "eating traffic" is a false positive. A full SADE diagnostic sweep across all layers found zero evidence of any device failure or traffic loss.

**Affected component:** None — no subsystem, daemon, interface, or policy is misconfigured in a way that breaks observed traffic.

**Mechanism:** The user's report does not match any observable signal. Both r6 and r7 are fully operational: their ospfd processes are running, they hold Full OSPF adjacencies with multiple peers (r6: 3 Full neighbors on eth0/eth1/eth2; r7: 1 Full neighbor on eth0), and each carries 57–59 active OSPF routes. End-to-end reachability between pc0 (20.1.1.10) and pc12 (120.1.1.10) is 0% loss in both directions, confirming that transit traffic through the core is reaching its destination without issue.

**Localization:** The ospf_snapshot flagged two minor observations — r13 has no ospfd running, and r8 declares an orphaned OSPF area 2 — but neither constitutes a fault. r13 carries no ospfd in its watchfrr daemon list and has zero OSPF configuration, making it a static-route-only leaf router by design. r8's area 2 (networks 18/8 and 80/8) has no peer routers because domain BB is a single-device stub; r8 still maintains Full adjacencies in area 1 and the backbone via virtual link.

**Root cause:** No fault exists. The alarm was triggered in error; the current state of the network is entirely healthy.

**Fix:** No corrective action is required. Do not reboot any device. Investigate the monitoring alert rule that generated the false alarm to prevent recurrence.

The agent's log contains concrete tool outputs (reachability sweep, infra/l2/ospf snapshots, ps and vtysh on relevant routers) that directly support the final conclusion that core routers R6/R7 are healthy and end-to-end traffic is fine. Inference steps are logical and the investigation covers the necessary layers to rule out the reported fault.
